chunks: "I'd characterize it on three axes: compute, memory and efficiency, and then check which one the workload actually hits. Compute first.
Peak FLOPS is the number of FP32 lanes times two, because a fused multiply-add is two operations, times the clock. A GPU with 80 SMs, 128 lanes each at 1.
7 gigahertz is about 35 TFLOPS. Then memory bandwidth: a 256-bit GDDR6 bus at 16 Gb/s per pin is 512 GB/s. Divide the two and you get the ridge point, about 68 FLOP per byte.
A kernel below that intensity is memory-bound, so a vector add or SAXPY gets under one percent of peak no matter how many cores you have.
A big matrix multiply with good tiling is far above it and can approach peak.
For graphics I'd add pixel and texel fill rates and, importantly, frame time, so I'd look at the 99th-percentile frame, not just average FPS, because stutter is what people notice.
Then efficiency: performance per watt, and achieved versus peak, meaning occupancy, divergence, coalescing.
And I'd always measure on my own workload, including host-to-device transfers, because a synthetic benchmark number can be nowhere near what my application sees."
